title: Ghanaian Egg Stew
author: Gabi Odebode
desc: Beaten egg poured into thickened tomato purée in sections and left alone until the surface turns white and the eggs almost set.
longDesc: Egg stew is breakfast and supper across much of West Africa, and the Ghanaian version is distinguished by using tomato alone where Nigeria adds bell pepper. Five plum tomatoes, garlic, onion and an optional habanero are blended and simmered covered ten to twelve minutes until thickened. Five eggs are beaten with bouillon and poured into the stew in sections without stirring, then covered on medium-low until the surface turns white and the eggs are almost set — about five minutes. Only then are they stirred into clusters and cooked uncovered another five.
equipment: Frying pan or saucepan with a lid
steps: Blend the tomatoes, garlic, onion and habanero.
Heat the oil and add the purée.
Simmer covered until thickened, 10 to 12 minutes.
Stir in 1 teaspoon of the bouillon powder.
Beat the eggs with the remaining bouillon.
Pour the eggs into the stew in sections, without stirring.
Cover on medium-low until the surface turns white and the eggs almost set, about 5 minutes.
Uncover, stir into clusters, and cook uncovered about 5 minutes more, until the liquid reduces.
chefTips: Pour the egg in sections and do not stir. That is the whole technique — it gives you clusters of set egg in sauce rather than a scramble.
Surface turning white and the eggs almost set is the cue, at about five minutes. Stirring before that point destroys the clusters.
Ten to twelve minutes covered on the tomato purée first. The stew must be thick before the egg goes in, or you get egg soup.
Tomato only, no bell pepper. The author is explicit that this is what separates the Ghanaian version from the Nigerian one.
Vegetable oil rather than palm oil, by the author's choice — she says palm oil can dominate. If you want it redder and richer, palm oil is the swap.
Bouillon is split between the stew and the beaten egg. Seasoning the egg itself is what stops the clusters tasting bland.
Salt only if needed, after the bouillon. Bouillon powder is already salty.
commonMistakes: Stirring the eggs in as soon as they are poured.
Adding the eggs before the purée has thickened.
Adding bell pepper, which makes it the Nigerian version.
All the bouillon into the stew, leaving the egg unseasoned.
sources: Adapted from 'Ghanaian Egg Stew', Food Network Kitchen, 24 October 2022. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Gabi Odebode'. Page metadata as printed: 4 servings, 30 minutes total, easy. Quantities confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS).

Ingredients exactly as printed: 5 plum tomatoes, roughly chopped; 4 cloves garlic, roughly chopped; 1 small onion, roughly chopped; 1 habanero pepper, stemmed, optional; 2 tablespoons vegetable oil; 2 teaspoons bouillon powder (preferably chicken); 5 large eggs; Kosher salt, if needed; Cooked yam, plantains or rice, for serving.

THE REGIONAL DISTINCTION, verbatim from the headnote and the reason this is filed as Ghanaian rather than pan-West African: 'Egg stew, also referred to as "egg sauce," is made in several West African countries… In Ghana, the stew is made with tomato puree, while in Nigeria, it is made with both tomatoes and bell peppers…'

THE AUTHOR'S OIL CHOICE, verbatim and declared: 'I… use vegetable oil instead of stronger-flavored palm oil, which can dominate.' That is an author's substitution rather than the traditional choice, and it is flagged as such.
DONENESS CUES, both quoted: 'simmer until thickened (10-12 minutes)'; and 'until surface turns white and eggs almost set (5 minutes)'.

Method as printed: blend the vegetables; simmer the purée covered until thickened, then stir in 1 teaspoon bouillon; beat the eggs with the remaining bouillon and pour into the stew in sections WITHOUT STIRRING; cover on medium-low until almost set; uncover, stir into clusters, and cook uncovered about 5 more minutes until the liquid reduces.

THE POUR-IN-SECTIONS-WITHOUT-STIRRING instruction is the technique that distinguishes this from scrambled eggs in sauce, and it is reproduced as the central step rather than smoothed into a general direction.
The same author's mpotompoto is published at GHA034.
storage: 2 days refrigerated. Egg stew does not keep well beyond that.
reheating: Low heat, briefly. Overheating makes the egg rubbery.
healthBenefits: Eggs are a complete protein and supply choline, vitamin D and B12.
Cooked tomato is high in lycopene, more bioavailable than raw.
Low in carbohydrate before the accompaniment.
culturalNote: Egg stew with boiled yam or fried plantain is one of the most common meals in Ghana — cheap, fast and made from things that keep without refrigeration. That the Ghanaian and Nigerian versions differ by exactly one ingredient, the bell pepper, is the kind of detail that only a cook who has made both would bother writing down.
